subject: social_science
chapter_title: Agriculture: Types of Farming, Cropping Seasons and Major Crops

concepts.title: Primitive Subsistence Farming and Slash and Burn
concepts.definition: A small-plot cultivation method that uses hand tools and household labour, where a cleared patch is burnt, cropped briefly, and abandoned once soil fertility declines so a new patch can be cleared.
concepts.key_idea: Known locally as jhumming in the north-east, bewar in Madhya Pradesh, podu in Andhra Pradesh, and by other regional names; productivity stays low without fertilisers or modern inputs.
question_patterns: what is slash and burn agriculture and why do farmers shift to a new patch
by what local names is primitive subsistence farming known in different states of India
explain two features of primitive subsistence farming
why is land productivity low under jhumming
which tools and labour are used in slash and burn cultivation
what are the world-wide names of shifting cultivation such as milpa and roca

solution_steps.explain: Check the markers: small patches, primitive tools like hoe, dao and digging sticks, family or community labour, dependence on monsoon and natural fertility.
Confirm the farmer clears and burns a patch, grows cereals for family needs, and moves on when fertility drops, letting nature restore the soil.
Match the region with its local term, for example jhumming in Assam and Meghalaya, dipa in Bastar, milpa in Mexico, roca in Brazil, ladang in Indonesia.

concepts.title: Intensive Subsistence Farming
concepts.definition: Labour-heavy cultivation on small inherited holdings in densely populated regions, where heavy doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation squeeze the maximum output from limited land.
concepts.key_idea: Right of inheritance fragments holdings into uneconomical sizes, yet farmers keep raising output from the same plots because they lack other livelihoods.
question_patterns: why is intensive subsistence farming labour intensive
how does the right of inheritance affect land holding size
why do farmers take maximum output from limited land in intensively farmed areas
distinguish intensive subsistence farming from primitive subsistence farming
which kind of population pressure leads to intensive subsistence farming
what role do biochemical inputs and irrigation play in intensive farming

solution_steps.explain: Confirm the area carries high population pressure on land, which makes farms small and labour abundant.
Look for high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation used to lift production from small plots.
Confirm inheritance-driven division has made holdings uneconomical, and the absence of alternative livelihoods keeps pressure on the land.

concepts.title: Commercial Farming and Plantation Agriculture
concepts.definition: Market-oriented cultivation that uses high doses of modern inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides to raise productivity, with plantation as its single-crop, large-area variant linking farm and factory.
concepts.key_idea: The same crop can be commercial in one region and subsistence in another, for example rice in Haryana and Punjab versus Odisha; plantations like tea in Assam need capital, migrant labour and strong transport links.
question_patterns: what are the main characteristics of commercial farming
how is plantation agriculture linked to industry
why does the degree of commercialisation vary from region to region
name the important plantation crops of India
why do plantations need a well developed network of transport and communication
how do HYV seeds and chemical fertilisers raise productivity in commercial farming

solution_steps.action: check input use and market orientation
solution_steps.explain: Confirm modern inputs like HYV seeds, fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides are used and the produce is meant for the market.
Compare whether the same crop is sold commercially in one region and grown for self-use in another, as rice is in Haryana and Punjab versus Odisha.
For plantations, confirm a single crop over a large tract, capital intensive inputs, migrant labourers, and produce flowing to processing industries through transport networks.

concepts.title: Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid
concepts.definition: India's farm calendar divides the year into three growing seasons: a winter sown rabi season, a monsoon sown kharif season, and a short summer zaid season lying between them.
concepts.key_idea: Rabi crops like wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard are harvested in summer; kharif crops like paddy, maize, jowar, bajra and cotton come with the monsoon; zaid covers watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and fodder.
question_patterns: distinguish between rabi and kharif crops with examples
when are rabi crops sown and harvested
name the crops grown in the zaid season
which states are important for rabi production and why
what are the three paddy crops of Assam West Bengal and Odisha
how do western temperate cyclones help rabi crops

solution_steps.action: place the crop in its season
solution_steps.explain: Match sowing and harvesting windows: rabi sown October to December and harvested April to June; kharif sown with the monsoon onset and harvested in September-October; zaid in the summer months between.
Verify the climate support, for example winter precipitation from western temperate cyclones for rabi, and monsoon rainfall for kharif paddy.
Confirm the producing regions, such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh for wheat, and Assam, West Bengal and coastal Odisha for rice with three paddy crops aus, aman and boro.

concepts.title: Major Food Crops: Rice, Wheat, Millets and Pulses
concepts.definition: India's staple cereals each need a specific temperature and rainfall band: rice demands heat above 25 degrees and over 100 cm rain, wheat needs a cool season with 50 to 75 cm rain, millets are hardy coarse grains, and pulses are protein-rich leguminous crops that fix nitrogen.
concepts.key_idea: Pulses except arhar restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen and are grown in rotation; jowar, bajra and ragi carry high nutrition; India is the largest producer and consumer of pulses.
question_patterns: describe the geographical conditions required for the growth of rice
which temperature and rainfall suit wheat cultivation
why are millets called coarse grains and why do they still matter
how do leguminous pulses help restore soil fertility
name the major producing states of jowar bajra and ragi
which pulse is an exception to nitrogen fixing

solution_steps.explain: Compare the crop's needs: rice above 25 degrees Celsius with over 100 cm rainfall; wheat a cool growing season with 50 to 75 cm rainfall and bright sunshine at ripening.
Match zones, for example the Ganga-Satluj plains and Deccan black soil for wheat, moist rain-fed tracts for jowar, sandy or shallow black soils for bajra, dry regions for ragi.
Check nutritional and agronomic traits: ragi rich in iron and calcium, pulses supplying protein and fixing atmospheric nitrogen except arhar, supporting rotation with other crops.

concepts.title: Beverage, Fibre and Cash Crops: Tea, Coffee, Cotton, Jute and Rubber
concepts.definition: Plantation beverages (tea and coffee) and industrial crops (cotton, jute, rubber, sugarcane, oil seeds) each carry distinct climate needs, from frost-free moist slopes for tea to equatorial humidity above 200 cm rain for rubber.
concepts.key_idea: Jute is the golden fibre of flood-plain soils; cotton needs 210 frost-free days on Deccan black soil; Arabica coffee from Baba Budan Hills grows in the Nilgiris; sericulture rears silkworms for silk.
question_patterns: name one important beverage crop and specify the geographical conditions required for its growth
why is jute called the golden fibre
which climatic conditions suit cotton cultivation
where was Arabica coffee introduced in India
what is sericulture
which rainfall and temperature does the rubber crop require
list the main oil seeds grown in India

solution_steps.explain: Tea needs warm moist frost-free weather, well-drained humus-rich soil and frequent showers; rubber needs over 200 cm rain and temperatures above 25 degrees; cotton needs high temperature, light rainfall and 210 frost-free days.
Classify the produce: beverages, gunny bags and ropes from jute, cotton textile raw material, cooking oils from groundnut and mustard, industrial raw material from rubber.
Confirm regions: Assam and Darjeeling for tea, Nilgiris in Karnataka Kerala and Tamil Nadu for coffee, West Bengal and Bihar for jute, Deccan states for cotton, Kerala and Garo hills for rubber.

concepts.title: Population Dependence on Agriculture
concepts.definition: Agriculture remains the livelihood backbone of the country, supporting roughly three-fifths of the people, so any estimate of the farm-dependent population scales directly with the total population and its dependence percentage.
concepts.key_idea: Because about 60 per cent of people live off farming, technical and institutional reforms decide the welfare of a very large population share.
question_patterns: calculate how many people depend on agriculture given the total population and dependence percent
find the farm dependent population for a country of given population
what share of India's population is engaged in agricultural activities
compute the number of people engaged in farming when the percentage is known
how much of the population does agriculture provide livelihood for

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the total population by the percentage of people engaged in agriculture and divide by 100

concepts.title: Oilseed Cropping Share of Cropped Area
concepts.definition: Oil seeds occupy roughly one-eighth of the gross cropped area, so the land under oilseeds can be worked out directly from the total cropped area using its percentage share.
concepts.key_idea: Different oil seeds cover about 12 per cent of the total cropped area; groundnut alone accounts for about half of the major oilseeds produced.
question_patterns: calculate the area under oil seeds from the total cropped area
find the cropped area covered by oilseeds given its percentage share
what proportion of the total cropped area do oil seeds cover
compute land under oilseed cultivation for a state with a known cropped area
which oil seed accounts for about half of the oilseeds produced

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the total cropped area by 12 and divide by 100 to get the land under oil seeds

concepts.title: Bhoodan Land Distribution per Villager
concepts.definition: In the Bhoodan movement a landowner donates a plot for the landless, and the plot is shared equally among the recipient villagers, so each villager's share equals the donated area divided by the number of landless villagers.
concepts.key_idea: Vinoba Bhave's movement began at Pochampally when Shri Ram Chandra Reddy offered 80 acres for 80 landless villagers; later zamindars donated whole villages as Gramdan.
question_patterns: calculate the share of land each landless villager receives from a bhoodan donation
find the per villager land share when donated area and number of villagers are given
who started the bhoodan gramdan movement and where
why is the bhoodan gramdan movement called the bloodless revolution
what is the difference between bhoodan and gramdan
how many acres were offered at pochampally and to how many villagers

solution_steps.explain: Divide the donated land by the number of landless villagers to get each person's share

concepts.title: Technological and Institutional Reforms in Agriculture
concepts.definition: Sustained gains in farming require institutional changes such as collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari, plus technical support like crop insurance, Grameen banks, Kisan Credit Card and minimum support prices.
concepts.key_idea: The Green Revolution and White Revolution (Operation Flood) raised output but concentrated gains in selected areas, prompting comprehensive land development programmes in the 1980s and 1990s.
question_patterns: enlist the institutional reform programmes introduced in the interest of farmers
suggest initiatives taken by the government to increase agricultural production
what were the strategies of the green revolution and white revolution
how do kisan credit card and personal accident insurance scheme help farmers
why was consolidation of holdings necessary after land reforms
how does minimum support price protect farmers from speculators and middlemen

solution_steps.explain: Separate institutional steps (land reform, zamindari abolition, consolidation, cooperation) from technical steps (package technology, irrigation, insurance, credit).
Match each measure to its farmer benefit: loans at lower interest from Grameen banks and cooperative societies, compensation through crop insurance, fair prices through minimum support price.
Place reforms in sequence: land reform in the First Five Year Plan, Green and White Revolutions in the 1960s and 1970s, comprehensive land development in the 1980s and 1990s.
